quotation: Must one be ordained to be a witness with us of his resurrection.
exegesis: Verses 21–22 specify the qualifications for replacing Judas among the Twelve; verses 23–26 record the selection of Matthias. Paul appeals to seeing Jesus in 1 Corinthians 9:1 and describes his appearance as exceptional in 15:8. Galatians 1:1 grounds his commission in Christ rather than human appointment.
evaluation: Acts 1 concerns the Twelve specifically, not every use of apostolos. Philippians 2:25 calls Epaphroditus a messenger. Neither broader usage nor missionary commissioning establishes equal revelatory authority.

quotation: And are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone;
language: θεμέλιος (themelios), foundation; ἐποικοδομηθέντες, aorist passive participle, having been built upon.
exegesis: 2:19 identifies a united household; 2:20 identifies its foundation; 2:21–22 describe continuing growth. The genitive may describe the foundation constituted or laid by the apostles and prophets. 3:5 connects them with revelation. In 4:11 Christ gives ministers; 4:12–16 states their equipping purpose.
evaluation: Continuationists appeal to the until clause in 4:13. It establishes the goal of ministry, but does not explicitly require every office to recur. The foundational role supplies the cumulative cessationist inference.

quotation: the prophet hath spoken it presumptuously
language: נָבִיא (navi), prophet; בְּזָדוֹן (bezadon), presumptuously; διακρινέτωσαν, let them evaluate.
exegesis: Moses distinguishes authorized speech from falsely attributed speech in verses 20–22. Jeremiah 18:7–10 qualifies conditional warnings. In 1 Corinthians 14:29–33 Paul regulates prophetic speech and testing within gathered worship.
evaluation: The command to evaluate prophecy does not itself specify whether errors belong to false claimants or fallible reports of revelation. Grudem proposes the latter; cessationists require positive textual warrant for that category. God’s speech is truthful; impressions are not automatically revelation.

quotation: All scripture is given by inspiration of God
exegesis: Paul urges Timothy to remain in the sacred writings learned from childhood (14–15); their divine origin and usefulness equip him for every good work (16–17). Hebrews contrasts former prophetic speech with climactic speech in the Son. Jude calls believers to contend for the faith once delivered.
evaluation: These texts establish authority, sufficiency and the settled gospel deposit; none independently gives a date for every gift’s cessation. Read alongside Ephesians 2 and apostolic qualifications.

quotation: dividing to every man severally as he will.
exegesis: Verses 4–6 connect diverse gifts with the same Spirit, Lord and God. Verse 7 identifies the common good; verse 11 establishes sovereign distribution. Verses 29–30 employ μή questions expecting negative answers. Hebrews 2:3–4 connects signs with divine attestation of the announced salvation.
evaluation: The attestation purpose does not prove every miracle ceased. Reject universal gift requirements while recognizing continuing service and God’s sovereign power.

quotation: But when that which is perfect is come, then that which is in part shall be done away.
language: τὸ τέλειον (to teleion), the complete or perfect; ἐκ μέρους, in part.
exegesis: Verses 8–10 contrast enduring love with temporary gifts and partial knowledge. Verse 11 uses childhood and maturity; verse 12 contrasts mirror-like sight with face-to-face knowledge. Verse 13 emphasizes love.
evaluation: The face-to-face language favors consummation. Neither a completed-canon reading nor a claim that every gift must operate continuously until consummation follows necessarily. Build cessationism cumulatively.

quotation: every man heard them speak in his own language.
language: γλῶσσα (glossa), tongue or language; διάλεκτος (dialektos), language or dialect.
exegesis: Acts 2:6–11 names peoples and recognizable languages. First Corinthians 14:21 cites Isaiah 28 in a judgment context; verses 22–25 contrast signs and intelligible speech; 27–28 limit speakers and require interpretation. 12:13 and 30 distinguish shared Spirit participation from universal tongues.
evaluation: The precise nature of all Corinthian tongues is debated. Even granting continuation, public practice must satisfy Paul’s conditions. Distinguish classical Pentecostal initial evidence from salvation requirements.

quotation: God, who quickeneth the dead, and calleth those things which be not as though they were.
language: καλοῦντος (kalountos), calling, a participle describing God.
exegesis: Romans 4:17 describes the God Abraham trusted; verses 19–21 focus on God’s ability to fulfill his promise despite human impossibility. James 4:13–16 rebukes presumptuous planning and directs believers to the Lord’s will. Proverbs 18:21 describes speech’s consequences in wisdom literature.
evaluation: The grammatical subject of creative calling is God, not Abraham. Trusting a divine promise differs from creating one through speech.

language: πίστιν θεοῦ (pistin theou), faith in God; genitive naturally understood as objective here.
exegesis: The withered fig tree frames Jesus’ instruction. Verses 23–24 encourage confident prayer; verse 25 connects prayer and forgiveness. Hebrews 11:35–38 includes faithful people who suffered and died; 39–40 locates fulfillment in God’s larger plan.
evaluation: Even if one proposes a different genitive reading, the context does not establish faith as an impersonal force. Compare 1 John 5:14 for prayer according to God’s will.

quotation: But godliness with contentment is great gain.
exegesis: Verse 5 condemns treating godliness as gain; verse 6 redefines gain through contentment. Verses 7–10 highlight transience and dangers of greed. Verses 17–19 instruct the wealthy to trust God and share. Philippians 4:12 describes hunger and abundance; verse 13 concerns strength in both.
evaluation: Neither text condemns wealth itself. Both contradict a universal entitlement to material prosperity and the interpretation of Philippians 4:13 as unlimited achievement.

quotation: by whose stripes ye were healed.
language: ἰάθητε (iathete), you were healed, aorist passive; חַבּוּרָה (chabburah), wound or stripe.
exegesis: Isaiah connects the servant’s suffering with sin and restoration. Matthew applies Isaiah 53:4 to Jesus’ physical healings. Peter applies the servant’s wounds to dying to sin and living to righteousness (2:24–25). Romans 8:23 places final bodily redemption in the future.
evaluation: Atonement secures ultimate bodily restoration, but does not guarantee immediate healing. Paul’s unanswered request (2 Corinthians 12:7–10) and Trophimus’s illness (2 Timothy 4:20) refute a universal claim. James 5 encourages prayer, not control.

quotation: beside me there is no God.
language: אֱלֹהִים (elohim), God or gods depending on context; κοινωνοί (koinonoi), participants.
exegesis: Psalm 82 portrays judged figures called gods, whose identity is debated (human rulers or heavenly beings). John 10:34–36 argues from that scriptural usage to the propriety of Jesus’ claim as the sanctified Son; 37–38 points to his works. Second Peter 1:4 connects participation with escaping corruption.
evaluation: Neither disputed reading of Psalm 82 makes believers possess the divine essence. Isaiah 43:10 and 44:6–8 exclude rival deity; participation is by grace, not ontological identity.

quotation: Whatsoever ye shall bind on earth shall be bound in heaven
language: δήσητε (desete), bind; λύσητε (lysete), loose; ἔσται δεδεμένα, future periphrastic perfect passive.
exegesis: Matthew 16 links keys to Peter’s confession. Matthew 18:15–17 outlines correction, witnesses and church discipline; verse 18 addresses the disciples in the plural. Verses 19–20 promise Christ’s presence in that setting.
evaluation: The perfect construction is compatible with heavenly authorization, but grammar alone does not settle every question of temporal priority. Context rules out unlimited power to decree desired circumstances.

quotation: Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law
exegesis: Ezekiel 18:2–4 challenges the sour-grapes proverb; verses 5–20 distinguish father and son by their conduct. Galatians 3:10–13 contrasts reliance on law with Christ bearing its curse; verse 14 identifies Abrahamic blessing and the Spirit through faith.
evaluation: Scripture recognizes intergenerational consequences, not a universal need for specialized curse-breaking rites. Colossians 2:13–15 grounds freedom in Christ’s work.

quotation: for God loveth a cheerful giver.
exegesis: Paul prepares a collection for needy saints. Verse 6 uses sowing and reaping; verse 7 rejects compulsion; verse 8 directs sufficiency to every good work. Verses 10–13 explain the harvest as righteousness, generosity and thanksgiving. Acts 8 condemns buying spiritual authority.
evaluation: Paul expects divine provision, not a contractual financial multiplier. The collection’s beneficiaries and stated purpose guard against treating offerings as investments.

quotation: My kingdom is not of this world
language: ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου τούτου (ek tou kosmou toutou), from this world; ἐκ marks source.
exegesis: Jesus contrasts his kingship with worldly coercion before Pilate; his servants are not fighting to prevent his arrest. Acts 1 redirects questions about restoration toward Spirit-empowered witness. Peter commands elders to shepherd without domineering.
evaluation: Christ’s kingdom source does not prohibit all civic engagement. It does undermine claims that new apostles receive coercive or extrabiblical jurisdiction over the church or society.

language: τετέλεσται (tetelestai), perfect passive indicative, it has been completed.
exegesis: John 19:28–30 links completion with fulfillment of Scripture and Jesus’ death. Luke 23:46 records entrusting his spirit to the Father. First Peter 3:18 contrasts death in flesh and life in spirit (interpretation disputed); Hebrews 9:14 describes Christ’s self-offering through the eternal Spirit.
evaluation: Penal substitution is real, including the suffering expressed in the cry of abandonment. It does not entail a rupture of the divine essence or regeneration of a spiritually sinful Christ. The eternal Son dies according to his human nature.
